## Why This Matters

L22 left two questions open. First, collaborative filtering is **blind to anyone new**: a brand-new
user has no ratings to find neighbors from, and a brand-new movie has no ratings to be a neighbor --
the **cold-start** problem. Second, the top-N lists *looked* reasonable, but looking reasonable is not
a measurement. This lesson supplies the rest of the recommender family -- the approaches that work with
*no* rating history -- and the discipline that tells you whether any recommender is actually any good.

## Content-Based Filtering

Collaborative filtering ignored *what* an item is. **Content-based filtering** does the opposite: it
recommends items whose **features** match the ones you liked. MovieLens tags every movie with 19
**genre** flags, so each movie is a 0/1 vector in "genre space." Build a user's **content profile** by
adding up the genre vectors of the movies they rated, weighted by how far above their own average each
rating was -- the genres they reliably like come out large and positive, the ones they dislike go
negative. Then score every unseen movie by the **cosine similarity** (L18) between its genre vector and
that profile.

![A horizontal bar chart of user 196's content profile across the 19 genres. Drama sticks out far to the right at about +5.2; Children, Fantasy, and Documentary are small and positive; Action at about -5.8, Adventure, Romance, Comedy, Sci-Fi, and War are negative. The chart shows one dominant liked genre and several disliked ones.](assets/l23_genre_profile.png)

The strength: content-based handles a **brand-new item** fine -- a movie just added still has genres,
even with zero ratings. The weakness, which you will see directly in the lab: **over-specialization**.
A Drama lover gets a list of nothing but Dramas; the method keeps serving the same flavor and rarely
surprises you. (Genres are also a coarse feature, so many movies tie on similarity -- the lab breaks
ties by popularity.)

## Demographic Filtering

**Demographic filtering** recommends by *who you are*. MovieLens ships real attributes in `u.user` --
age, gender, occupation -- so you can ask "what do women aged 25-34 rate highest?" and recommend that
to a new member of that cohort. It needs **no ratings from the target user at all**, which is exactly
why it can greet a brand-new user the moment they sign up. The cost is bluntness: everyone in a cohort
gets the same suggestions, and grouping people by demographics raises fairness questions (a theme for
Unit VIII).

## Knowledge-Based Filtering

**Knowledge-based filtering** skips history entirely and works from **stated rules and constraints**.
A travel site that asks your dates, budget, and climate, then applies rules to filter the catalog, is
recommending without a single past rating. In the lab you build a tiny version: "a highly-rated Comedy
from the 1990s" is a rule (genre = Comedy, year in the 90s, mean rating high enough, enough ratings to
trust). Knowledge-based systems shine for **rare, high-stakes, or first-time** purchases -- a house, a
mortgage, a laptop -- where nobody has a rating history and the user can state what they need.

## Hybrid Recommenders

No single family wins everywhere, so real systems **combine** them -- a **hybrid**:

- **Switching** -- use one approach until another becomes possible: greet a new user with demographic
  or popular picks, then **switch** to collaborative filtering once they have rated enough.
- **Weighted** -- **blend** several scores into one (e.g. average a content score and a collaborative
  score), so each covers the other's blind spots.

Every large platform ships a hybrid: it is the only way to be good for new users, new items, *and*
seasoned users at once.

## Cold Start, Resolved

Now the L22 table can be completed -- the *fix* for each gap is just "use a family that does not need
that history":

| Approach | Needs | New user | New item |
|----------|-------|----------|----------|
| **Collaborative filtering** | a ratings matrix | fails (no neighbors) | fails (no raters) |
| **Content-based** | item features | needs a few likes first | **works** (new item has features) |
| **Demographic** | user attributes | **works** (no ratings needed) | not applicable |
| **Knowledge-based** | stated rules | **works** (asks directly) | **works** |
| **Hybrid** | a mix | **works** (switch / blend) | **works** |

The standard playbook: start a new account with **demographic / popular** picks, lean on
**content-based** for fresh items, and shift to **collaborative filtering** as real ratings accumulate.

## How to Evaluate a Recommender

A list that looks plausible can still be wrong. To *measure* a recommender, hide some of the known
ratings (a **train/test split**, exactly as in L11), predict them, and compare the predictions with the
truth using two standard error metrics:

$$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n}\sum (\hat r - r)^2}, \qquad \text{MAE} = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum \lvert \hat r - r \rvert$$

**RMSE** (root mean squared error) squares each miss, so it punishes big misses hardest; **MAE** (mean
absolute error) is the plain average miss, in stars. Lower is better for both. Run them on the methods
you built in L22 and a clear **accuracy ladder** appears:

![A bar chart titled "Each idea predicts ratings a little better." Four bars of test RMSE, lower being better: global mean 1.124 and item mean 1.021 in gray as simple baselines, item-item collaborative filtering 0.945 in blue, and matrix factorization 0.922 in green. The bars step downward from left to right; an annotation marks CF and matrix factorization as the methods built in L22.](assets/l23_rmse_ladder.png)

**Reading the output:** each idea beats the one before. Knowing the global average already gets you to
1.124; knowing *which movie* (item mean) helps; knowing how *similar users or movies* rate (collaborative
filtering) helps more; and **matrix factorization** -- the Netflix-Prize family from L22, here with 20
latent factors per user and movie -- wins at **0.922**. This is the ladder behind that \$1M prize.

## Rating Error vs. Ranking Quality

One honest caveat. RMSE and MAE score how well you predict a *rating*, but what a user actually
experiences is the *ranking* -- did the right items reach the top of the list? A model can shave RMSE
yet reorder the top 10 for the worse. Ranking is measured differently, with metrics like
**precision@k** (of the top k you showed, how many did the user like?). We name it here and use a
ranking lens in the L24 project; the key idea is that **predicting ratings well and ranking items well
are related but not the same goal.**

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Which approach is best?"** None alone -- the right answer is almost always a **hybrid**. The
interesting question is not "which method" but "which method *for which situation*" (new user, new item,
rich history).

**"Isn't more data enough?"** More ratings help collaborative filtering, but they do nothing for a user
who has rated *nothing* -- cold start is a structural gap, not a volume problem -- and they cannot fix a
mismatch between optimizing RMSE and optimizing what users actually want.

**"Is offline RMSE the final word?"** No. Offline metrics are how you *screen* ideas cheaply; the real
test is an **online A/B test** on live users, because recommendations change the very behavior you
measure. (Online evaluation is beyond this course; we name it so you know the offline number is a
start, not the verdict.)

## Ethics

Demographic filtering groups people by age, gender, or region -- convenient, but it can encode and
amplify bias, and "people like you" can quietly become "people boxed in like you." Content-based
over-specialization is how **filter bubbles** form. Optimizing a single offline number (watch time,
clicks) is how engagement-at-any-cost systems arise. **Unit VIII** takes these up directly.

## Key Takeaways

- **Content-based** uses item features (genres), handles new items, but over-specializes.
- **Demographic** uses user attributes and **demographic** / **knowledge-based** approaches need no
  rating history -- they cover the **cold start** that breaks collaborative filtering.
- **Hybrid** systems (switching or weighted) combine families to be good for new users, new items, and
  veterans at once -- what every platform ships.
- **Evaluate** with a held-out split: **RMSE** (punishes big misses) and **MAE** (average miss). The
  ladder: popularity -> item -> collaborative filtering -> matrix factorization, each a little better.
- **RMSE/MAE measure rating prediction; ranking quality (precision@k) is a related but different goal.**

## Cheat-sheet

| Task | Idea |
|---|---|
| Content profile | rating-weighted sum of the liked items' feature vectors |
| Content score | cosine(profile, item-feature vector) |
| Demographic pick | top-rated items within a user cohort (`groupby` attributes) |
| Knowledge-based pick | filter the catalog by stated rules (genre, year, min rating) |
| Hybrid | switch between families, or blend their scores |
| Evaluate | `train_test_split`, then RMSE \( \sqrt{\text{mean}((\hat r - r)^2)} \) and MAE |
